slides.title: What are Type I and Type II errors?

shapes.alt: Fair spinner with three equal sectors, one marked Win and two marked Lose.

transcription.tex: Anirudh plays a game in which he spins a fair 3-sided spinner and gets 1 point if it lands on ‘WIN’. He spins the spinner 10 times and gets 7 points. His friends think he might have cheated (e.g. tampering with the spinner to favour a win).\par Let $X$ count wins. Test $H_0:p=1/3$ against $H_1:p>1/3$. At the 10% level the critical region is $X\ge6$, since $P(X\ge6)=0.0766$ and $P(X\ge5)>0.10$ under $H_0$.
What if a fair spinner gives seven wins?

Seven lies in the rejection region. The friends would reject $H_0$ even though the spinner is fair. This is a false positive.\par The probability of this error for a fair spinner is $P(X\ge6\mid p=1/3)=0.0766$, the actual significance level.
What if a biased spinner gives five wins?

Five falls outside the rejection region. The friends have insufficient evidence of bias even though the spinner favours a win. This is a false negative.\par Its probability is $P(X\le5\mid p)$ for the true $p>1/3$. A number can be calculated once $p$ is specified.

slides.title: Decisions and the two types of error

transcription.tex: Which hypothesis is actually true?
$H_0$ is true
$H_1$ is true
Do not reject $H_0$
\textbf{Correct decision}\par True negative. A healthy patient tests negative.
\textbf{Type II error}\par False negative. A patient with the disease tests negative.
Reject $H_0$
\textbf{Type I error}\par False positive. A healthy patient tests positive.
\textbf{Correct decision}\par True positive. A patient with the disease tests positive.
For the diagnostic example, the null hypothesis is that the patient does not have the disease. A test result and the patient’s actual condition play different roles.

slides.title: Testing for a reduction in accidents

transcription.tex: Accidents occurred on a stretch of motorway at an average rate of 6 per month. Many of the accidents that occurred involved vehicles skidding into the back of other vehicles. By way of a trial, a new type of road surface that is said to reduce the risk of vehicles skidding is laid on this stretch of road, and during the first month of operation 4 accidents occurred.\par (a) Test this result to see if it gives evidence that there has been an improvement at the 5% level of significance.\par (b) Calculate P(Type I error) for this test.\par (c) If the true average rate of accidents occurring with the new type of road surface was 3.5, calculate the probability of a Type II error.
The critical region stays fixed. To calculate a Type II error, change the accident rate and use the region outside the critical region.

Let $X$ count accidents in one month. Test $H_0:\lambda=6$ against $H_1:\lambda<6$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(6)$.\par $P(X\le4)=0.2851>0.05$. Four accidents give insufficient evidence of an improvement.
$P_6(X\le1)=0.01735$, but $P_6(X\le2)=0.06197>0.05$. Reject for $X\le1$.\par The actual Type I error probability is $0.01735$.
If $\lambda=3.5$, a Type II error occurs for $X\ge2$.\par $P_{3.5}(X\ge2)=1-e^{-3.5}(1+3.5)=0.8641$.

slides.title: A two-tailed test for a biased coin

transcription.tex: A coin is spun 20 times and a head is obtained on 7 occasions.\par (a) Test, at the 5% significance level, to see whether or not the coin is biased.\par (b) Calculate the probability of a Type I error for this test.\par (c) Given that the coin is biased and that this causes the tail to appear 3 times for each head that appears, calculate the probability of a Type II error for the test.
Split the 5% significance level equally between the two tails. Six more heads have the same significance as six fewer heads for a fair coin.

Test $H_0:p=0.5$ against $H_1:p\ne0.5$. Under $H_0$, the number of heads $X\sim\mathrm B(20,0.5)$.\par $P(X\le5)=P(X\ge15)=0.020695$ and $P(X\le6)>0.025$. Reject for $X\le5$ or $X\ge15$. Seven is outside both tails. There is insufficient evidence of bias.
The two tails are disjoint. $P(\mathrm{Type\ I})=2P_{0.5}(X\le5)=0.04139$.
Three tails per head gives $p=1/4$. A Type II error occurs when $6\le X\le14$.\par $P_{0.25}(X\le14)-P_{0.25}(X\le5)=0.3828$.

Jane knows from experience that 10% of the emails she receives are spam. After her email service upgraded the spam filters, she recorded the number of emails sent up to and including the first spam email. She wants to test, at the 5% significance level, whether this upgrade improved the spam filter.\par (a) Find the critical region for her test.\par (b) Calculate the probability of a Type I error for this test.\par (c) Given that after the upgrade the probability of an email she receives being spam is now 1 in a 100, calculate the probability of a Type II error for the test.
For trials up to and including the first success, $P(X\ge n)=(1-p)^{n-1}$ and $P(X\le n)=1-(1-p)^n$.

Let $X$ count emails up to and including the first spam email. Test $H_0:p=0.1$ against $H_1:p<0.1$. A better filter makes the wait longer.\par Under $H_0$, $P(X\ge c)=0.9^{c-1}\le0.05$. Taking logs and reversing the inequality gives $c\ge1+\log(0.05)/\log(0.9)$. The first integer is 30.
If $p=0.01$, a Type II error means the first spam email occurs within 29 emails.\par $P_{0.01}(X\le29)=1-0.99^{29}=0.2528$.
Question 10

\textbf{a} Define:\par (i) a Type I error\par (ii) a Type II error.\par The discrete random variable $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(p)$. You wish to test $H_0 : p = 0.004$ against $H_1 : p \ne 0.004$, using a 10% significance level. The probability in each tail should be as close to 0.05 as possible.\par \textbf{b} Find the critical region for this test.\par \textbf{c} State the probability of a Type I error occurring for this test.

\textbf{a} (i) A Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is rejected.\par (ii) A Type II error occurs when a false null hypothesis is not rejected.\par \textbf{b} Under $H_0:p=0.004$, $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.004)$. The alternative $H_1:p\ne0.004$ calls for two tails, each as close as possible to 0.05.\par Upper tail: $P(X\ge a)=0.996^{a-1}$. Solving $0.996^{a-1}<0.05$ gives $a-1>\log(0.05)/\log(0.996)$, so $a>748.434$.\par Compare the neighbouring cut-offs: $P(X\ge748)=0.996^{747}=0.050087$ and $P(X\ge749)=0.996^{748}=0.049887$. The first is closer to 0.05.\par Lower tail: $P(X\le b)=1-0.996^b$. Solving $1-0.996^b<0.05$ gives $0.996^b>0.95$, hence $b<\log(0.95)/\log(0.996)=12.798\ldots$.\par $P(X\le12)=0.04696$ and $P(X\le13)=0.05077$. The second is closer. The critical region is $X\le13$ or $X\ge748$.\par \textbf{c} Add the two disjoint tails under $H_0$. $P(\text{Type I error})=0.05077+0.05009=0.1009$ (4 d.p.).
Question 11

Michael has bought a dice with 20 sides, and his friend David suspects that it is landing on 17 more often than it is landing on the other values. They both decide to test this in two different ways, using a 5% significance level. Michael throws the dice 40 times and records the number of times the dice lands on the 17.\par \textbf{a} Find the critical region for Michael’s test.\par \textbf{b} State the probability of a Type I error occurring for Michael’s test.\par David decides to throw the dice until the first time it lands on 17.\par \textbf{c} Find the critical region for David’s test.\par \textbf{d} State the probability of a Type I error occurring.\par The actual probability of the dice landing on 17 is 0.0588.\par \textbf{e} Calculate the probability of a Type II error occurring in David’s test.\par \textbf{f} Calculate the probability of a Type II error occurring in Michael’s test.

\textbf{a} Let $p$ be the chance of rolling 17. Test $H_0:p=0.05$ against $H_1:p>0.05$. For Michael's count $X$, under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm B(40,0.05)$.\par Seek an upper tail of at most 5%. $P(X\ge4)=1-P(X\le3)=1-0.8619=0.1381$.\par $P(X\ge5)=1-P(X\le4)=1-0.9520=0.0480$. Thus the critical region is $X\ge5$.\par \textbf{b} $P(\text{Type I error})=P(X\ge5\mid p=0.05)=0.0480$.\par \textbf{c} For David's waiting time, under the same $H_0$, $Y\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.05)$. A larger $p$ gives a shorter wait. We need $P(Y\le c)=1-0.95^c\le0.05$.\par Hence $0.95^c\ge0.95$. Taking logs and dividing by $\log(0.95)<0$ gives $c\le1$. The critical region is $Y=1$.\par \textbf{d} $P(\text{Type I error})=P(Y=1\mid p=0.05)=0.05$.\par \textbf{e} Under $p=0.0588$, $Y\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.0588)$. David fails to reject if the first roll misses: $P(Y>1)=1-0.0588=0.9412$.\par \textbf{f} For Michael, $X\sim\mathrm B(40,0.0588)$. By calculator $P(\text{Type II error})=P(X\le4)=0.9162$ (4 d.p.).

slides.title: Two tails for a normal mean

transcription.tex: Bags of sugar having a nominal weight of 1 kg are filled by a machine. From past experience it is known that the weight, $X$ kg, of sugar in the bags is normally distributed with a standard deviation of 0.04 kg. At the beginning of each week a random sample of 10 bags is taken in order to see if the machine needs to be reset. A test is then done at the 5% significance level with ${H}_{0}:\mu =1.00$ kg and ${H}_{1}:\mu \ne 1.00$ kg. Find:\par (a) the critical region for this test.\par (b) $P($Type 1 error$)$ for this test.\par Assuming that the mean weight has in fact changed to 1.02 kg.\par (c)    find $P($Type II error$)$ for this test.
A normal distribution is continuous. We can choose the critical values to give exactly 2.5% in each tail. Keep the unrounded limits in the next calculation.

Under $H_0$, $\bar X\sim N(1,0.04^2/10)$. Put $s=0.04/\sqrt{10}$. Standardise using $Z=(\bar X-1)/s$.\par With $z=\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$, reject below $L=1-zs\approx0.975208$ or above $U=1+zs\approx1.024792$ kg.
When $\mu=1.02$, $\bar X\sim N(1.02,s^2)$. A Type II error occurs between the same limits.\par $\Phi((U-1.02)/s)-\Phi((L-1.02)/s)=0.6474$.

The weight of jam in a jar, measured in grams, is distributed normally with a mean of 150 g and a standard deviation of 6 g. The production process occasionally leads to a change in the mean weight of jam per jar but the standard deviation remains unaltered.\par The manager monitors the production process and for every new batch takes a random sample of 25 jars and weighs their contents to see if there has been any reduction in the mean weight of jam per jar.\par Find the critical values for the test statistic $\overline{X}$, the mean weight of jam in a sample of 25 jars, using:\par (a) a 5% level of significance\par (b) a 1% level of significance\par Given that the true value of $\mu $ for the new batch is in fact 147,\par (c)    find the probability of a Type II error for each of the above critical regions.
Use the same standard error for both tests. A smaller significance level moves the lower critical value further from the null mean.
Test $H_0:\mu=150$ against $H_1:\mu<150$. Under $H_0$, $\bar X\sim N(150,6^2/25)$. Its standard error is $1.2$ g.\par $c_5=150+1.2\Phi^{-1}(0.05)=148.0262$ g. Reject for $\bar X\le c_5$.
Question 4

A manufacturer claims that the average outside diameter of a particular washer produced by his factory is 15 mm. The diameter is assumed to be normally distributed with a standard deviation of 1 mm. The manufacturer decides to take a random sample of 25 washers from each day’s production in order to monitor any changes in the mean diameter.\par \textbf{a} Using a significance level of 5%, find the critical region to be used for this test.\par Given that the average diameter had in fact increased to 15.6 mm,\par \textbf{b} find the probability that the day’s production would be wrongly accepted.

\textbf{a} Test $H_0:\mu=15$ against $H_1:\mu\ne15$. Under $H_0$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm N(15,1/25)$.\par $Z=(\bar X-15)/(1/5)=5(\bar X-15)$. Put 2.5% in each tail of the 5% test: reject for $Z<-1.96$ or $Z>1.96$.\par Solving $5(\bar X-15)=\pm1.96$ gives limits 14.608 and 15.392 mm. Reject for $\bar X<14.608$ or $\bar X>15.392$.\par \textbf{b} Accepting the day's production when the mean is actually 15.6 is a Type II error. Now $\bar X\sim\mathrm N(15.6,1/25)$.\par $P(14.608\le\bar X\le15.392)=P(\bar X\le15.392)-P(\bar X<14.608)$.\par By calculator this is $0.1492-0.0000=0.1492$ (4 d.p.).
Question 5

The number of patients that a medic can inoculate with a vaccine in one day can be modelled by a normal distribution with mean 40 and standard deviation 8. The manufacturer of the vaccine claims that a new method of inoculation will speed up the rate at which the medic works.\par A random sample of 30 medics tried out the new method of inoculation and the average number of patients they dealt with per day $\bar X$ was recorded.\par \textbf{a} Using a 5% significance level, find the critical value of $\bar X$.\par The average number of patients dealt with per day using the new method of inoculation was in fact 42.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability of making a Type II error.\par The manufacturer of the vaccine would like to lessen the probability of a Type II error being made and recommends that the significance level be changed. c State, giving a reason, what recommendation you would make.

\textbf{a} Test $H_0:\mu=40$ against $H_1:\mu>40$. Under $H_0$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm N(40,8^2/30)$.\par $Z=(\bar X-40)/(8/\sqrt{30})=\sqrt{30}(\bar X-40)/8$. The upper 5% critical value is 1.6449.\par Solve $\sqrt{30}(c-40)/8=1.6449$. Thus $c=40+1.6449(8/\sqrt{30})\approx42.4025$.\par \textbf{b} When $\mu=42$, use $\bar X\sim\mathrm N(42,8^2/30)$. The Type II error is failing to reject: $P(\bar X\le42.4025\mid\mu=42)=0.6086$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} Increase the significance level. This reduces the upper critical value of $Z$ and the threshold for $\bar X$. When the new method really improves the mean, the probability of falling below that threshold decreases.
Which hypothesis is actually true?
$H_0$ is true
$H_1$ is true
Do not reject $H_0$
\textbf{Correct decision}\par Probability $1-\alpha$ under $H_0$.
\textbf{Type II error}\par Probability $\beta$ at the specified alternative.
Reject $H_0$
\textbf{Type I error}\par Probability $\alpha$. This is the size of the test for a simple null hypothesis.
\textbf{Correct decision}\par Probability $1-\beta$. This is the power at the specified alternative.
Each column adds to one. To calculate the size or power, use the rejection region in both cases. Change the parameter to match the hypothesis you are considering.

slides.title: Size and power of a binomial test

transcription.tex: The random variable $X$ has a binomial distribution. A random sample of size 25 was taken to test ${H}_{0}:p=0.30$ against ${H}_{1}:p<0.30$ using a 10% level of significance.\par (a) find the critical region for this test.\par (b) find the size of this test.\par Given that $p=0.20$,\par (c)    calculate the power of this test.
Size and power both use the critical region. For size calculate with the null parameter. For power calculate with the specified alternative.
Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm B(25,0.30)$. The alternative $p<0.30$ gives a lower-tail test.\par $P_{0.30}(X\le4)=0.09047$ while $P_{0.30}(X\le5)=0.19349$. At 10%, reject for $X\le4$.
The size is the probability of rejection under $H_0$: $P_{0.30}(X\le4)=0.09047$.
At $p=0.20$ use the same critical region with $X\sim\mathrm B(25,0.20)$. The power is $P_{0.20}(X\le4)=0.42067$.

Jam is sold in jars. The amount of jam, in grams, in a jar is normally distributed with mean $\mu $ and standard deviation 5. The manufacturer claims that $\mu $ is 106 and quality control officers will take action against the manufacturer if $\mu <106$. A random sample of 30 jars is examined and a 5% level of significance is used.\par (a) find the critical region for the sample mean using this test.\par Given that in fact $\mu =102$,\par (b)    find the power of this test.
Keep the critical mean from part (a) to calculate the probability of rejection in part (b).

Test $H_0:\mu=106$ against $H_1:\mu<106$. The standard error for the sample mean is $s=5/\sqrt{30}$.\par Under $H_0$, $\bar X\sim N(106,s^2)$. At the lower 5% point, $(c-106)/s=\Phi^{-1}(0.05)$.\par $c=106+s\Phi^{-1}(0.05)=104.49846\ldots$ g. Reject for $\bar X<c$.
At $\mu=102$, $\bar X\sim N(102,s^2)$.\par $P_{102}(\bar X<c)=\Phi((c-102)/s)=0.9969$. A sample of 30 jars is very likely to detect this reduction.

A particular mobile-phone provider fails to deliver text messages with probability \(p\).\par Brooke wants to investigate whether \(p>0.02\).\par Using \({H}_{0}:p=0.02\) and \({H}_{1}:p>0.02\), Brooke notes the number of text messages she is able to send successfully up until the first failure. If this value is less than or equal to 5 she rejects \({H}_{0}\). If it is more than 100 she accepts \({H}_{0}\). If it is more than 5 but less than or equal to 100 she notes the number of additional text messages she is able to send successfully up until the next failure. She rejects \({H}_{0}\) if this is less than or equal to 5 and accepts it otherwise.\par Find the size of this test.\par Calculate the power of this test when \(p=0.015\).
For $X$ counting the failed send, $P(X>n)=(1-p)^n$ and $P(X\le n)=1-(1-p)^n$.

Let $X$ count sends up to and including the first failure. The question counts successful sends before that failure, so its count is $X-1$. For independent sends, $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(p)$.\par Under $H_0$, $p=0.02$. Reject immediately if $X\le6$: $a=1-0.98^6\approx0.11416$.\par Take a second sample if $6<X\le101$: $b=0.98^6-0.98^{101}\approx0.75588$.\par The probability of rejection on that independent sample is again $a$. The two rejection paths give size $a+ba\approx0.20045$.

At $p=0.015$, the probability of rejection on a single short wait is $a=1-0.985^6\approx0.08669$.\par The probability of taking a second sample is $b=0.985^6-0.985^{101}\approx0.69601$.\par $g(0.015)=a+ba\approx0.14703$. This is the rejection probability at the requested value. Since $0.015<0.02$, that value lies outside the stated alternative.
Question 4

A manufacturer claims that a particular rivet produced in his factory has a diameter of 2 mm, and that the diameter is normally distributed with a variance of 0.004 $\mathrm{mm}^2$.\par A random sample of 25 rivets is taken from a day’s production to test whether the mean diameter had altered, up or down, from the stated figure. A 5% significance level is to be used for this test.\par If the mean diameter had in fact altered to 2.02 mm, calculate the power of this test.

Test $H_0:\mu=2$ against $H_1:\mu\ne2$. Under $H_0$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm N(2,0.004/25)$.\par $Z=(\bar X-2)/\sqrt{0.004/25}=5(\bar X-2)/\sqrt{0.004}$. A two-tailed 5% test has 2.5% in each tail, so reject for $|Z|>1.96$.\par Solve $5(c-2)/\sqrt{0.004}=\pm1.96$. The limits are $1.97521$ and $2.02479$ mm. Reject outside them.\par When $\mu=2.02$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm N(2.02,0.004/25)$. Power is the sum of both rejection probabilities:\par $P(\bar X<1.97521)+1-P(\bar X\le2.02479)\approx0.0002+1-0.6475=0.3527$.
Question 5

In a binomial experiment consisting of 10 trials the random variable $X$ represents the number of successes, and $p$ is the probability of a success.\par In a test of $H_0 : p = 0.3$ against $H_1 : p > 0.3$, a critical region of $x\ge7$ is used.\par Find the power of this test when\par \textbf{a} $p = 0.4$\par \textbf{b} $p = 0.8$.\par \textbf{c} Comment on your results.

\textbf{a} For $p=0.4$, $X\sim\mathrm B(10,0.4)$. Power is $P(X\ge7)=1-P(X\le6)=1-0.9452=0.0548$.\par \textbf{b} For $p=0.8$, $X\sim\mathrm B(10,0.8)$. Let $Y=10-X$ count failures, so $Y\sim\mathrm B(10,0.2)$. Power is $P(X\ge7)=P(Y\le3)=0.8791$.\par \textbf{c} The test is more powerful at 0.8. Both values are above the null value 0.3. As $p$ increases, seven or more successes become more likely.
Question 6

Explain briefly what you understand by\par \textbf{a} a Type I error (1 m\par \textbf{b} the size of a significance test. (1 m\par A single observation is made on a random variable $X$, where $X\sim\mathrm N(\mu,10)$.\par The observation, $x$, is to be used to test $H_0 : \mu = 20$ against $H_1 : \mu > 20$. The critical region is chosen to be $x\ge25$.\par \textbf{c} Find the size of the test.

\textbf{a} A Type I error occurs when the null hypothesis is true and the test rejects it.\par \textbf{b} The size of a test is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, namely $P(\text{Type I error})$.\par \textbf{c} The rejection region is $X\ge25$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm N(20,10)$, with standard deviation $\sqrt{10}$.\par Size $=P(X\ge25\mid\mu=20)=1-\Phi((25-20)/\sqrt{10})=1-0.9431=0.0569$ (4 d.p.).
Question 9

The wallpaper produced by a certain manufacturer has defects that occur randomly at a constant rate of $\lambda$ per roll. If $\lambda$ is thought to be greater than 0.8 then action has to be taken.\par Using $H_0: \lambda = 0.8$ and $H_1: \lambda > 0.8$, a quality control manager takes a sample of 10 rolls and rejects $H_0$ if there are 12 or more defects. If there are 9 or fewer defects then $H_0$ is accepted. If there are 10 or 11 defects, a second sample of 10 rolls is taken and $H_0$ is rejected if there are 8 or more defects in this second sample, otherwise it is accepted.\par \textbf{a} Find the size of this test.\par b\par Find the power of this test when $\lambda = 1$.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ and $Y$ count defects in the first and second independent samples of ten rolls. Under $H_0$, each has distribution $\mathrm{Po}(10\times0.8)=\mathrm{Po}(8)$.\par Reject straight away if $X\ge12$, or after the second sample if $10\le X\le11$ and $Y\ge8$. The routes are disjoint.\par Size $=P(X\ge12)+P(10\le X\le11)P(Y\ge8)$.\par Write $F(k)=P(X\le k)$. Then size $=1-F(11)+[F(11)-F(9)][1-F(7)]$\par $=1-0.8881+(0.8881-0.7166)(1-0.4530)=0.1119+0.1715(0.5470)=0.1119+0.0938=0.2057$.\par \textbf{b} When $\lambda=1$ per roll, $X,Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(10)$. Evaluate the same two disjoint ways to reject, now using the cumulative probabilities with mean 10.\par Power $=1-0.6968+(0.6968-0.4579)(1-0.2202)$\par $=0.3032+0.2389(0.7798)=0.3032+0.1863=0.4895$.
Question 10

A sweet manufacturer makes boxes of jelly beans. The number of jelly beans in each box is assumed to be normally distributed with standard deviation 5.\par A consumer group wants to test the manufacturer’s claim that the mean number of jelly beans in each box is 80. The group takes repeated samples of 20 boxes and records the mean number of jelly beans per box in each sample.\par The random variable $X$ represents the number of samples the group need to take before they obtain a sample with a mean less than 79.\par If $X\le10$ the group rejects the company’s claim.\par \textbf{a} Find the size of this test.\par \textbf{b} Given that the actual mean number of jelly beans in each box is 81, find the power of this test.

\textbf{a} Let $Y$ count beans in one box and $\mu$ be the population mean. For 20 boxes, $\bar Y\sim\mathrm N(\mu,25/20)$.\par Under $H_0:\mu=80$, a qualifying sample has probability $p=P(\bar Y<79)=0.185547\ldots$.\par The waiting time to the first qualifying sample is $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(p)$. Reject at $X\le10$. Size $=P(X\le10\mid\mu=80)=1-(1-0.185547\ldots)^{10}=1-0.128428\ldots=0.8716$.\par \textbf{b} At $\mu=81$, $p=P(\bar Y<79)=0.036819\ldots$. The probability of rejecting is\par $P(X\le10\mid\mu=81)=1-(1-0.036819\ldots)^{10}=1-0.68719\ldots=0.3128$.

Fix a test and its rejection region $C$. If the underlying rate is $\lambda$, the power function is $g(\lambda)=P_{\lambda}(X\in C)$.\par At the null value this gives the actual significance level. At an alternative value it gives the chance of detecting that change.

shapes.alt: Illustrative power function increasing as the rate increases from three to nine.

transcription.tex: Choose a value on the horizontal axis. Read up to the curve, then across to the probability of rejection.\par In this upper-tail example, a larger true rate puts more probability in the rejection region. The test has greater power to detect larger increases.\par For example, $g(5)\approx0.50$ means that, at that rate, about half of repeated tests reject the null hypothesis.

slides.title: A power function for accident counts

transcription.tex: Past experience has shown that the number of accidents that take place at a road junction has a Poisson distribution with an average of 3.5 accidents per month. A trading estate is built along one of the roads leading away from the junction and the local council is anxious that this may have increased the accident rate. To see if the number of accidents had increased, a test was set up with the null hypothesis ${H}_{0}:\lambda =3.5$ and with the alternative hypothesis being accepted if the number of accidents $X$ within the first month after the alteration was $\ge 7$.\par (a) Find the size of the test.\par (b) Find the power function for the test and sketch the graph of the power function.
If an exam gives a partially completed table, calculate the missing powers for the specified rates and plot those points.
Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(3.5)$. Reject at $X\ge7$.\par Size $=1-P_{3.5}(X\le6)=1-0.9347=0.0653$.

$g(\lambda)=P_\lambda(X\ge7)=1-P_\lambda(X\le6)$.\par $g(\lambda)=1-e^{-\lambda}\left(1+\lambda+\frac{\lambda^2}{2!}+\frac{\lambda^3}{3!}+\frac{\lambda^4}{4!}+\frac{\lambda^5}{5!}+\frac{\lambda^6}{6!}\right)$.\par $g(4)=0.1107$, $g(5)=0.2378$, $g(6)=0.3937$. Plot each value against its rate. The curve rises towards one.

transcription.tex:
A manufacturer of sweets supplies a mixed assortment of chocolates in a jar. He claims that 40% of the chocolates have a ‘hard centre’, the remainder being ‘soft centred’.\par A shopkeeper does not believe the manufacturer’s claim and proposes to test it using the following hypotheses.\par \({H}_{0}:p=0.4,\hspace{1.12em}{H}_{1}:p<0.4\)\par where \(p\) is the proportion of ‘hard centres’ in the jar. Two tests are proposed.\par In test \(A\) he takes a random sample of 10 chocolates from the jar and rejects \({H}_{0}\) if the number of ‘hard centres’ is less than 2.\par (a) Find the size of test \(A\).\par (b) Show that the power function of test \(A\) is given by 
\({\left(1-p\right)}^{10}+10p{\left(1-p\right)}^{9}\)\par In test B he takes a random sample of 5 chocolates from the jar and if there are no ‘hard centres’ he rejects \({H}_{0}\), otherwise he takes a second sample of 5 chocolates and \({H}_{0}\) is rejected if there are no further ‘hard centres’ on this second occasion.\par (c) Find the size of test \(B\).\par (d) Find an expression for the power function of test \(B\).\par The powers for test \(A\) and test \(B\) for various values of \(p\) are given in the table.\par \[\begin{array}{c|ccccc}p&\text{0.1}&\text{0.2}&\text{0.25}&\text{0.3}&\text{0.35}\\\text{Power for test }A&\text{0.74}&r&\text{0.24}&s&\text{0.09}\\\text{Power for test }B&\text{0.83}&\text{0.54}&\text{0.42}&\text{0.31}&\text{0.22}\end{array}\]\par (e) Calculate values for \(r\) and \(s\).\par (f) State, giving a reason, which of the two tests the shopkeeper should use.
A test can gain power by rejecting more often. Compare its false-positive risk at the same time.
At $p=0.4$, let $q=0.6^5$ be the chance of no hard centres in five. Reject on the first sample or take a second independent sample and reject there.\par Size $=q+(1-q)q\approx0.14947$.
Now $q=(1-p)^5$. The same two disjoint rejection paths give\par $g_B(p)=q+(1-q)q=2(1-p)^5-(1-p)^{10}$.

Test B detects a real reduction more often at every value in the table. Its false-positive risk is also greater: about 14.95%, compared with 4.64% for A.\par Choose B if detecting a shortfall is the priority. If the false-positive risk must stay below 5%, choose A.

slides.title: Testing a change in fox sightings

transcription.tex: A local park believes the fox population in the area has decreased. They want to test for the probability $p$ that a fox will be observed on any given day. They count the number of days, $X$, that pass until the first observation of a fox. They test ${H}_{0}:p=0.1$ against ${H}_{1}:p<0.1$ and reject ${H}_{0}$ if $X>30$.\par (a) Find the size of the test.\par (b) Find the power function of the test.
The event $X>30$ means the first 30 days have no sighting. Day 31 is the earliest sighting in this event.
Under $H_0:p=0.1$, $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.1)$. Reject when $X>30$.\par The size is $P_{0.1}(X>30)=0.9^{30}=0.04239$.

At any specified $p$, independent days have probability $1-p$ of no sighting. Thus $g(p)=P_p(X>30)=(1-p)^{30}$.\par For $p<0.1$, rarer sightings make long waits more likely, so the power increases as $p$ decreases.
Question 1

A single observation $x$ is taken from a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda$.\par This observation is to be used to test $H_0:\lambda=6.5$ against $H_1:\lambda<6.5$. The critical region chosen was $x\le2$.\par \textbf{a} Find the size of the test.\par \textbf{b} Show that the power function of this test is given by $e^{-\lambda}(1+\lambda+\tfrac12\lambda^2)$\par The table gives the value of the power function to two decimal places.\par $\begin{array}{|c|r|r|r|r|r|r|}\hline \lambda&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline\text{Power}&0.92&s&0.42&0.24&t&0.06\\\hline\end{array}$\par \textbf{c} Calculate values for $s$ and $t$.\par \textbf{d} Draw a graph of the power function.\par \textbf{e} Find the values of $\lambda$ for which the test is more likely than not to come to the correct conclusion.

\textbf{a} Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(6.5)$. For the given lower-tail test $P(X\le3)=0.1118$ and $P(X\le2)=0.0430$. The latter lies below 0.05. Its size is $P(X\le2\mid\lambda=6.5)=0.0430$.\par \textbf{b} $P(X\le2)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)=e^{-\lambda}+e^{-\lambda}\lambda/1!+e^{-\lambda}\lambda^2/2!$.\par Hence the power function is $g(\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}(1+\lambda+\lambda^2/2)$.\par \textbf{c} At $\lambda=2$, $s=5e^{-2}=0.68$ (2 d.p.). At $\lambda=5$, $t=(37/2)e^{-5}=0.12$ (2 d.p.).\par \textbf{d} Plot the tabulated points and draw the decreasing power curve.

shapes.alt: Power plotted at six integer means. Read across from power 0.5, then down to a Poisson mean of about 2.67.

transcription.tex: \textbf{e} At $\lambda=6.5$ the correct decision is to retain $H_0$, with probability $1-0.0430=0.9570>0.5$. For $\lambda<6.5$ the correct decision is to reject $H_0$.\par Read where the curve is above 0.5. The graph gives a crossing near 2.65. Solving $g(\lambda)=0.5$ more precisely gives $2.674\ldots$. The test is more likely than not to decide correctly for $0<\lambda<2.674\ldots$ or $\lambda=6.5$. The degenerate case $\lambda=0$ also gives certain rejection if a zero rate is allowed.

studentGraph.alt: Axes for the power against the Poisson mean

transcription.tex: Question 2

In a binomial experiment consisting of 12 trials, $X$ represents the number of successes and $p$ the probability of a success.\par In a test of $H_0: p = 0.45$ against $H_1: p < 0.45$ the null hypothesis is rejected if the number of successes is 2 or less.\par \textbf{a} Find the size of this test.\par \textbf{b} Show that the power function for this test is given by $(1-p)^{12}+12p(1-p)^{11}+66p^2(1-p)^{10}$\par c\par Find the power of this test when $p$ is 0.3.

\textbf{a} $H_0:p=0.45$, $H_1:p<0.45$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm B(12,0.45)$. The size is $P(X\le2\mid p=0.45)=0.0421$ (4 d.p.) from the binomial tables.\par \textbf{b} In general the power is $P(X\le2\mid p)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)$\par $=\binom{12}{0}(1-p)^{12}+\binom{12}{1}p(1-p)^{11}+\binom{12}{2}p^2(1-p)^{10}$.\par Since $\binom{12}{2}=12(11)/2=66$, this is $(1-p)^{12}+12p(1-p)^{11}+66p^2(1-p)^{10}$.\par \textbf{c} From the binomial tables, $P(X\le2\mid p=0.3)=0.2528$.\par Alternatively substitute $p=0.3$ in the power function: $0.7^{12}+3.6(0.7)^{11}+5.94(0.7)^{10}=0.2528$ (4 d.p.).
Question 4

A certain gambler always calls heads when a coin is spun. Before he uses a coin he tests it to see whether or not it is fair and uses the following hypotheses: $H_0: p = \frac12$ $H_1: p < \frac12$\par where $p$ is the probability that the coin lands heads on a particular spin. Two tests are proposed.\par In test A the coin is spun 10 times and $H_0$ is rejected if the number of heads is 2 or fewer.\par \textbf{a} Find the size of test A.\par \textbf{b} Explain why the power of test A is given by $(1-p)^{10}+10p(1-p)^9+45p^2(1-p)^8$\par In test B the coin is first spun 5 times. If no heads result, $H_0$ is immediately rejected. Otherwise the coin is spun a further 5 times and $H_0$ is rejected if no heads appear on this second occasion.\par \textbf{c} Find the size of test B.\par \textbf{d} Find an expression for the power of test B in terms of $p$.\par The power for test A and the power for test B are given in the table for various values of $p$.\par $\begin{array}{c|rrrrrr}p&0.1&0.2&0.25&0.3&0.35&0.4\\\hline\text{Power for test A}&0.9298&0.6778&&0.3828&&0.1673\\\text{Power for test B}&0.8323&0.5480&0.4183&0.3079&0.2186&0.1495\end{array}$\par \textbf{e} Find the power for test A when $p$ is 0.25 and 0.35.\par \textbf{f} Giving a reason, advise the gambler about which test he should use.

\textbf{a} For test A, $X\sim\mathrm B(10,p)$ and the critical region is $X\le2$. Size $=P(X\le2\mid p=0.5)=0.0547$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Power is $P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)$, using $X\sim\mathrm B(10,p)$.\par This gives $\binom{10}{0}(1-p)^{10}+\binom{10}{1}p(1-p)^9+\binom{10}{2}p^2(1-p)^8$.\par Since $\binom{10}{2}=10(9)/2=45$, the result is $(1-p)^{10}+10p(1-p)^9+45p^2(1-p)^8$.\par \textbf{c} For test B, each block of five spins has a binomial count $Y\sim\mathrm B(5,p)$. Under $H_0$, the probability of no heads in one block is $q=0.5^5=0.03125$.\par Reject after the first block, or continue and then reject. By independence the size is $q+(1-q)q=0.03125+(1-0.03125)0.03125=0.0615$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{d} Now $q=(1-p)^5$. Power $=(1-p)^5+[1-(1-p)^5](1-p)^5=(1-p)^5[2-(1-p)^5]$.\par \textbf{e} From the binomial tables, or part (b), $P(X\le2\mid p=0.25)=0.5256$ and $P(X\le2\mid p=0.35)=0.2616$.\par \textbf{f} For every alternative value in the table, test A has the greater power. On that evidence the gambler should use test A.
Question 6

A cyclist uses new tyres every time he does a time trial. He has found that on one specific route he has a probability of 0.9 of not getting a flat tyre. After changing tyre brands he believes that the new tyres are more resistant, and decides to perform a test, with 5% significance level, by doing 10 trials on the route and seeing how many times he would complete it without a flat tyre.\par \textbf{a} Find the size of the test.\par \textbf{b} Find the power function of the test.\par \textbf{c} Find the power function for the test if, instead of 10 trials, he had done 12 trials.\par \textbf{d} Given that the probability of completing the trial without a flat tyre with the new brand is 0.95, calculate which number of trials gives a more accurate test result.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count trials completed without a flat tyre. Test $H_0:p=0.9$ against $H_1:p>0.9$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(10,0.9)$.\par An improvement would give a large $X$. The smallest non-empty upper tail contains only the best possible result, ten successes.\par $P(X=10\mid H_0)=0.9^{10}=0.3487>0.05$. Every other non-empty upper tail is larger. The rejection region must therefore be empty. The actual size is $0$.\par \textbf{b} For every $p$, the probability of entering an empty rejection region is zero. Hence the power function is $g_{10}(p)=0$.\par \textbf{c} For twelve trials, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(12,0.9)$ under $H_0$. Even twelve successes have probability $0.9^{12}=0.2824>0.05$. The rejection region is again empty, so $g_{12}(p)=0$.\par \textbf{d} At $p=0.95$ the new tyres are better. The correct decision would be to reject $H_0$. Its probability is $g_{10}(0.95)=g_{12}(0.95)=0$. Neither number of trials gives a more accurate test result.
